To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a method for inactivation of chromosomally encoded genes in E. coli K 12 by using PCR products.
PCR products with extensions of about 40 nt can be used to inactivate chromosomal genes in E. coli by using the lambda Red system.

we have developed a simple, efficient method to disrupt genes in E. coli that uses primers with extensions that provide homology to the gene(s) of interest and PCR products that contain resistance genes flanked by FLP recognition target sites.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and use of PCR based methods to inactivate chromosomal genes in bacteria.
the development of new tools for the genetic analysis of bacteria.

the study of the molecular biology of bacteria, especially the enteric pathogen Escherichia Coli, which causes many diseases, including gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, meningitis, septicemia and other infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is a very efficient and easy way to inactivate a gene in E. coli.

this procedure is a powerful tool for gene inactivation, and it is especially useful when the gene is essential for cell viability or when the gene is located in a region that is difficult to manipulate by other methods.
the Red system can be used to inactivate chromosomal genes of any length in a variety of bacteria, including E. coli, Salmonella, and Streptomyces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a simple method for one-step inactivation of chromosomally encoded genes using PCR products.

the Red recombination system can be used to inactivate chromosomal genes in E. coli K12 using PCR products that are generated by using two sets of primers, one of which has 36-50 bp extensions that are homology to regions adjacent to gene to be inactivate and a plasmid that carries a resistance gene that is flanked by FLP recognition target (FRT) sites.
we have developed a simple method to disrupt chromosomally-encoded genes in bacteria by using PCR products as the source of homology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of PCR products as recombination templates is an extremely efficient way to disrupt chromosomal loci.
the Red system provides an efficient means of inactivating a gene of interest, and the FLP system provides an efficient method of removing the resistance gene.
PCR primers provide all of the homology necessary to inactivate chromosomal genes and that the procedure can be used in wild type cells.
